1.pericope_label: Jonathan and his armour-bearer climb between Bozez and Seneh and rout the Philistine outpost

schools.summary: Henry grants the maxim that it is nothing to God to save by many or by few readily in general and finds the difficulty in applying it: to believe that God can not only save us but save by us, when we are few and feeble, is the instance of faith that shall obtain a good report. He takes Rimmon for the strong rock in which six hundred Benjamites once sheltered and supposes Saul hidden in that very rock, so mean and abject was his spirit now that he had fallen under God’s displeasure. On the sending for priest and ark he is severe: a deserted prince courting a deserted priest, who would not make him wait nor reprove him as Samuel had done; many love to have such ministers as will prophesy smooth things to them, and those who have lost the substance of religion are fondest of its shadows. Of Jonathan he observes that great and generous souls are animated by opposition, that he threw himself on Providence in the choice of his sign, believing that God has the governing of the hearts and tongues of all men even of those who know him not, and that God will direct the steps of those who acknowledge him with full purpose of heart to follow his guidance. On the panic he notes that the original calls it a trembling of God, supernatural and irresistible, and that he who made the heart knows how to make it tremble.

Gill reconstructs the timing from Josephus, who says it was daylight when the two came up to the Philistine camp: the proposal was therefore probably made in the night and the pair set out by night, arriving at break of day. He corrects the genealogy of the priest, since Ahitub and not Ahiah was Ichabod’s brother, Ahiah being Ahitub’s son. He reports Abarbanel’s view that Jonathan spoke to his armour-bearer a second time, the young man having given no answer at first through fear. On the climb he has Jonathan turn aside from the pass the Philistines kept and go up a precipice thought inaccessible, coming on them unseen, and explains that he went on hands and feet not so much to avoid being seen as because he could not otherwise have got up at all; some think the rock was Bozez, which the Targum derives from its being lubricous and slippery.

Ellicott makes Jonathan the typical warrior of a wild and adventurous age, recklessly brave and generous, animated by an intense faith in the willingness and power of the Eternal to help Israel — the mainspring, he says, of the victorious power of every great Hebrew hero from Joshua and Gideon to David, and the thing King Saul utterly lacked, hence his rejection. He sets the son’s deed in deliberate contrast to the father’s conduct at Gilgal, quotes Bishop Hall on the divine power of faith that makes a man more than men, holds that the Spirit of the Lord plainly descended on him though the narrative does not say so, and notes that he never communicated his purpose to his father. He explains the ephod as the high-priestly garment with the breast-plate and the Urim and Thummim rather than the ordinary linen vestment, and judges the names of the two crags of extreme antiquity and their meaning disputed, possibly shining and the acacia, the rocks having been identified by modern travellers. Keil and Delitzsch take Rimmon for an appellative noun, a pomegranate-tree, and deny that the rock Rimmon is meant; they treat the clauses from the mention of the father down to the description of the crags as parenthetical, the thread being resumed by the repetition of Jonathan’s words; they map the topography from Robinson’s observation of the side wadys that supply the several crossings; they allow that Ahimelech may have been Ahiah’s brother who succeeded him, Ahiah having died without sons; and they judge the sign well chosen and no tempting of God, since Jonathan acted in the exercise of his calling and not for himself. On the trembling they have the ground quake with the noise and tumult of the frightened foe, the whole growing into a trembling of God, a supernatural terror miraculously infused.

Clarke says plainly that the action was totally contrary to the laws of war, no military operation being undertaken without the general’s knowledge, and allows it only as led by a divine influence; he traces the word for armour-bearer to the origin of esquire, gives the Targum’s glosses on the two crags as slippery and treading down, identifies Ahiah with Ahimelech, grounds the enlightening of the eyes in the dimming effect of hunger and fatigue, sets the asked sign beside the one Abraham’s servant requested, and thinks the trembling of the earth probably a metaphor for a great commotion, allowing that God might have produced a real earthquake. Wesley guards the topography of the pass against a natural misreading: the two rocks were not one on each hand, or Jonathan could have walked between them, but one toothed northward toward Michmash and the other southward toward Gibeah, so that he had to climb over both because the common ways were obstructed. He identifies Ahiah with Ahimelech and the ephod as the high priest’s with the Urim and Thummim, reads the appeal to their uncircumcision as a way of strengthening faith by reflecting that his enemies were God’s, notes that divers such extraordinary impulses were found among great and good men in ancient times, and ascribes the Philistines’ mutual slaughter to a God-sent panic that infatuated their minds.

debates.question: Is the Rimmon under which Saul waited a pomegranate-tree or the rock Rimmon?

positions.view: An appellative noun, a pomegranate-tree; the rock Rimmon is not meant
The strong rock in which six hundred Benjamites once sheltered
A tree, the love of trees being common in Israel
Yes, and the literal sense is far the best; the powers of nature were summoned as at the Red Sea and Beth-horon
The ground shook with the noise and tumult of the frightened foe
Probably a metaphor for a great commotion, though God might have produced a real one

debates.question: Was Ahiah the priest the same man as Ahimelech?

positions.view: Yes; the two names are forms of one, friend of the Eternal and brother of the king
Probably, but Ahimelech may instead have been his brother, succeeding him because he died without sons

outliers.claim: Alone in stating flatly that the enterprise was contrary to the laws of war, no operation being undertaken without the general’s knowledge.
Alone in correcting the picture of the pass, that the two crags stood north and south rather than one on each hand, so that both had to be climbed.
Alone in reconstructing the hour of the venture from Josephus, with the proposal made by night and the arrival at break of day.

Bozez and Seneh
come up to us and we will shew you a thing
twenty men within half an acre

16.pericope_label: The rout seen from Gibeah, the oracle broken off, and the turncoat Hebrews joining the pursuit

schools.summary: Henry offers two readings of the order to withdraw the hand and guards against a third: either the king thought the case plain enough now, or he would not wait for an answer, being in such haste to fight a falling enemy; but he would have been very unwise indeed if he forbade the lifting up of hands in prayer, since Moses continued to lift up his while Joshua was engaged with Amalek. A little thing, he adds, will divert a vain and carnal mind from religious exercises, and he that believeth will not make such haste as to reckon any business too urgent to take God along with him. He turns the enemy’s advantage against them, since they had been secure because all the swords and spears were theirs and God made their own weapons the instruments of their destruction, as he had done before in Israel’s wars. He notes that the people were cried together for want of the silver trumpets, that the deserters who had gone over recovered the hearts of Israelites when they saw the Philistines falling, and that those who had hidden in the mountains gained little praise by appearing so late, though it would have been more their reproach not to appear at all.

Gill places the watchmen in the highest part of Gibeah, which was built on a hill and took its name from it, so that they could overlook the Philistine camp and observe its motions. He notes that the Septuagint reads bring the ephod in place of the ark, and that Kimchi understood it of the ephod with the Urim and Thummim, the high priest putting it on to inquire concerning Jonathan’s doing and the agitation in the host. He takes the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines for servants and bondsmen, or men of the cities where they dwelt, or deserters from Israel who had gone over to the stronger party for safety and subsistence, and reports the Greek reading the servants. Of the victory he says it was wonderful that two men should throw so vast an army into confusion, and that it was a free favour bestowed on an undeserving prince who had behaved ill to his prophet at Gilgal and now to his high priest at Gibeah.

Ellicott sets out at length the case for reading ephod rather than ark. The Septuagint has bring hither the ephod, for he bore the ephod in those days; no hint anywhere suggests the sacred coffer left Kiriath-jearim before David bore it to Zion; the verb used here is never used of the ark; and no oracle could be asked of or by the ark, the Urim and Thummim by which answers were given belonging to the high-priestly ephod. He concludes that the Greek probably represents the original, that the present Hebrew is nevertheless of extreme antiquity, and that the explanatory second clause is most likely an ancient scribe’s gloss, noting that Josephus had the shorter text before him since he has the priest take the garment of his high priesthood and prophesy. He reports and rejects Maurer’s defence of the Hebrew, that the king wanted not an oracle but the encouragement of the ark’s presence, as sinking him to the level of the sons of Eli who carried the ark out and lost it. He judges the Rabbinical rendering of the obscure clause about the melting multitude the best, gives the distance between the camps as about two miles with a deep ravine between, takes the Hebrews with the Philistines for prisoners compelled to fight or levies raised where Philistine influence reached, and sees in the words for the mustering not a trumpet call but the raising of the war-cry, the king’s band penetrating wedge-like into the broken host. Keil and Delitzsch are struck by the same expression about the ark and press the same improbability, that it was then at Kirjath-jearim and would hardly be in so small a camp, and that elsewhere the high priest inquiring of God is associated with the ephod. They survey the readings of the obscure clause — the Rabbins unanimous for more and more was it broken up, Gesenius for dissolved and scattered, others adverbially for hither and thither as the Septuagint has it — render the order to the priest as draw thy hand in, and explain the two national names, those absorbed into the Philistine army being called Hebrews after the foreign usage and those with Saul called Israel after the sacred name.

Clarke reports the Vulgate’s quite different sense of the watchmen’s report, that the multitude were prostrate, and observes that where the Hebrew has Hebrews the Septuagint read slaves, so that its text must have had a word differing by a single letter — a reading, he adds, countenanced by no other version and no manuscript yet discovered. He also notes that the Vulgate and Septuagint add here that there were with Saul about ten thousand men, supported by no other authority. Wesley allows that the Hebrews went with the Philistines either by constraint, as servants, or in policy, to gain their favour and protection, and on the closing verse makes the same remark as Henry, that the Lord saved Israel and did it by them, for without him they could do nothing, salvation being of the Lord.

debates.question: Did Saul call for the ark or for the ephod?

positions.view: For the ephod, with the Septuagint and Josephus; the present Hebrew clause is probably an ancient scribe’s gloss
The ark reading is improbable, since it lay at Kirjath-jearim and inquiry elsewhere is tied to the ephod
The Greek reads ephod, and Kimchi understood the ephod with the Urim and Thummim
Take the text as it stands; he wished to inquire what use to make of the favourable moment

debates.question: What does the order to withdraw the hand mean?

positions.view: Either that he thought the case plain or that he would not wait for an answer — but not a forbidding of prayer, since Moses prayed on while Joshua fought
Simply draw thy hand in, that is, leave off now

debates.question: Who were the Hebrews that had been with the Philistines?

positions.view: Servants and bondsmen, or deserters gone over to the stronger party
Prisoners compelled to fight, or levies raised where Philistine influence reached
Either constrained as servants or acting in policy to gain protection
The Septuagint read a different word, slaves rather than Hebrews, though no other witness supports it

Alone in defending the priest’s prayer against the order to withdraw the hand, by the precedent of Moses praying on while Joshua fought Amalek.

24.pericope_label: Saul’s oath against eating, the honey in the wood, and the people’s eating with the blood

schools.summary: Henry allows the king the power to bind his soldiers with such an order and allows a good intention behind it, lest the people plunder and glut themselves on the deserted camp and lose time in the pursuit; then he condemns the act on three counts. It was impolitic, for what it gained in time it lost in strength. It was imperious, being worse than muzzling the ox that treads out the corn, since to forbid feasting would have been commendable but to forbid tasting, however hungry the men, was barbarous. And it was impious, for enforcing a military order with a curse and an oath, when superiors may chide and correct their inferiors but may not curse them, our rule being to bless and curse not; he wonders whether the cursing enemy of the Psalm was Saul. He observes that those are worthy of the name of Israelites who can deny their appetites when the delights of sense are most tempting, that many a good son has been entangled by the rashness of an inconsiderate father, and that daily work cannot be done without daily bread. On the evening’s greed he says two hungry meals make the third a glutton, notes that the cattle were slain on the ground instead of being hung up so the blood might run out, and faults the king for reproving the people without reflecting that he had been accessory and had made the Lord’s people transgress. On the altar he remarks that Saul was turning aside from God and yet began now to build altars, most zealous, as many are, for the form of godliness while denying its power.

Gill takes the altar for a place of peace offerings in thankfulness for the victory, or of sin offerings to atone for the people’s transgression, and settles on both with the former chiefly in view. He credits those who told the king of the eating with blood with being the more conscientious and religious sort, who strictly attended to the laws forbidding it and were concerned at the indecent behaviour of the rest.

Ellicott has the king so intent on vengeance, so bent on pursuing to the uttermost the Philistines who had long defied his power and brought him low, that he grudged his soldiers the necessary rest and refreshment and devoted to death with a terrible vow any who should slack his hand even to take food; he notes that the Septuagint inserts before the verse a long addition putting the force at about ten thousand men, a figure he thinks not improbable given the auxiliaries and the returning fugitives, and saying outright that Saul committed a great error. He explains the honey from the habit of wild bees filling hollow trees until the combs break with their own weight, renders the phrase literally a stream of honey, reads the enlightening of the eyes as the mere passing of the dimness of exhaustion, and quotes the Talmud’s prescription built on the verse, that whoever suffers from intense hunger should eat honey and other sweet things as efficacious to restore the light of the eyes. He quotes Dean Stanley’s comparison of the evening rush on the cattle to Mussulmans at sunset in Ramazan, finds in the rough expedient of the stone a proof that the king would have the Law of Moses honoured even in the direst necessity, and draws from it the judgement that Saul was a strangely complex character, now superstitiously watchful lest the letter of the Law be broken and now recklessly careless of God’s most solemn commands. On the altar he prefers the margin, that this was what he began to build as an altar, and reports the great Jewish commentators divided, Abarbanel holding that the king began but did not finish and the Midrash that he began among the kings of Israel the building of altars. Keil and Delitzsch are harshest on the oath, calling it no proper attitude towards the Lord but an act of false zeal and a despotic measure, and finding the proof in the wording, since the words about avenging himself upon his enemies show more regard to his own kingly power than to the cause of the kingdom of God; they note that the people took the oath by saying amen. They set out the two readings of the enlightened eyes, the written text probably giving that the eyes became seeing and recovered their power of vision while the Masoretes substituted a reading from the root meaning to become bright, which is likely correct since the letters are easily transposed. They render the rebuke as a charge of acting faithlessly towards Jehovah by transgressing the laws of the covenant, explain the stone as the means of letting the blood run off upon the ground, and doubt the altar was meant for sacrifice at all, taking it rather for a memorial of the revelation of God in so marvellous a victory.

Clarke treats the oath as a miscalculation: fearing the enemy would escape while the men refreshed themselves, the king made the taking of food before sunset a capital crime, and this was the very means of defeating his own intention, since the exhausted people could not continue the pursuit and there would otherwise have been a greater slaughter. He reports honey dews as not uncommon in most countries and says he has himself seen honey in considerable quantity on trees and long grass and often eaten of it, grounds the enlightened eyes in the dimming of sight by hunger and fatigue which food removes at once, calls the eating with blood another bad effect of the rash adjuration, reads the great stone as an altar on which the animals might be properly slain and the blood poured out, and notes of the altar that Samuel as prophet had hitherto erected them and that the king thought he had authority to erect one without the prophet, as he had once sacrificed without him. Wesley is the mildest judge of the oath: the intention was good and the matter of the obligation not simply unlawful, had it not been so rigorous in excluding all food and in binding the people under pain of an accursed death, a punishment far exceeding the fault. He notes that bees make their hives in trunks and clefts and holes of the earth, eminently so in Canaan, and puts the evening’s transgression in an epigram, that they who made conscience of the king’s commandment for fear of the curse made no scruple of transgressing God’s; of the rebuke he adds that the king sees their fault but not his own in giving the occasion of it.

debates.question: How far is Saul’s oath to be condemned?

positions.view: The intention was good and the matter not simply unlawful, only too rigorous and the penalty far beyond the fault
A miscalculation that defeated its own end, the exhausted people being unable to pursue
Impolitic, imperious and impious — above all for enforcing a military order with a curse
No proper attitude towards the Lord but an act of false zeal and a despotic measure, as the words about avenging himself show

debates.question: What is the reading behind the enlightened eyes?

positions.view: The written text gives that the eyes became seeing; the Masoretic reading from the root meaning to become bright is probably correct, the letters being easily transposed
It means only that the dimness of extreme exhaustion passed; literally his eyes became bright
A matter of physiology, hunger and fatigue dimming the sight and food removing the affection at once

debates.question: What does it mean that this was the first altar Saul built?

positions.view: Read with the margin, that he began to build it; Abarbanel has him begin without finishing, the Midrash has him begin the building of altars among the kings of Israel
It was his first altar, and probably no place of sacrifice but a memorial of the revelation of God in the victory
For peace offerings in thankfulness, or sin offerings to atone, and chiefly the former
The first he built, Samuel having hitherto erected the altars; he thought he might do it without the prophet

outliers.claim: Alone in reporting from his own observation that he has seen honey in quantity on trees and long grass and often eaten of it.

Alone in quoting the Talmud’s dietary prescription built on this verse, and alone in drawing from the stone the verdict that Saul was a strangely complex character, now scrupulous for the letter and now careless of the substance.

36.pericope_label: The silent oracle, the lot that took Jonathan, and the people’s rescue of him from his father’s vow

schools.summary: Henry takes the plain inference from the silence, that when God denies our prayers it concerns us to inquire what sin has provoked him, since his ear is not heavy but sin separates between us and him. He notes the king swore by his Maker that whoever was the Achan who troubled the camp should die, little thinking who the man was, and that none of the people answered because none who knew would inform. He knows both renderings of the prayer before the lot, that God would make a full discovery or that he would show the innocent, takes either as an air of impartial justice, and holds that lots are a solemn appeal to Providence and should be cast with prayer, which is why some have condemned games depending purely on chance as making too bold with a sacred thing. Of the lot falling where it did he says Providence designed to countenance a lawful authority and honour public justice, reserving another way to bring off one who had done nothing worthy of death. He faults the sentence on three counts: it was passed hastily without consulting the oracle, though Jonathan had a good plea in arrest of judgment, the act not being wrong in itself and the prohibition unknown to him; it was passed in fury, and justice is debased when administered with wrath and bitterness; and it was backed with a curse upon himself which returned on his own head, for Jonathan escaped and Saul was rejected and made anathema. He praises Jonathan’s submission, that he might have pleaded invincible ignorance or his own merit and instead yielded with a great and generous mind, it being as brave to yield in some cases as in others to fight; and of the rescue he says the people opposed their oath to the king’s and prevailed not by violence but by reason and resolution, Josephus adding that they prayed Jonathan might be loosed from the curse. He suspects the father was willing enough to have done for him what he would not do himself, and that he who knows the heart of a father knows not how to blame him.

Gill reports Abarbanel’s view that the king’s words were not the form of an oath at all but the asseveration of a curse that would befall him, namely that God would not answer him when he inquired and would do so again and again if Jonathan did not die. He has the people moved by grief, pity and sympathy for Jonathan, as Josephus observes, and explains the abandonment of the pursuit by the loss of time and opportunity spent examining his son’s case and casting lots to find it out.

Ellicott makes the priest the only man in that victorious army who dared, with the bravery which alone proceeds from righteousness, to withstand an imperious sovereign: he doubted whether the wholesale bloodshed certain to follow a night pursuit accorded with the will of God, no command to exterminate these Philistines having been given, and that day’s glory being wholly due to the interposition of the Eternal Friend of Israel. He treats the phrase for asking counsel as the technical term for inquiry by the Urim and Thummim, explains the silence as the questioner’s conclusion that a public transgression had been committed and needed special atonement, pictures the chiefs summoned round the rough unfinished altar in the dark night, glosses the word for chief of the people as literally corner stones, quotes Ewald on the ominous silence of a horror-stricken people, prefers the margin’s show the innocent as the better and more accurate rendering while giving give a perfect lot as Kimchi’s, cites Dean Payne Smith on the English Version’s readings having good authority in Jewish literature while neglecting the higher authority of the ancient versions, dismisses the long Greek addition as containing no fact of additional interest, and observes at the close that the king came to see the fault was his own and not his son’s. Keil and Delitzsch say the king was to perceive that guilt rested on the people, on account of which the Lord had turned away his countenance, and that the curse had to be brought to light as a warning; they gloss the word for the heads of the people, explain the repeated particles in the oath as emphatic, attribute the people’s silence to terror at the king’s word, render the prayer before the lot as a request that God give innocence or truth, print the Alexandrian addition in full as a paraphrase on the course pursued in casting lots, and hold the objection raised by the people so conclusive that Saul was obliged to yield — what Jonathan had done not being wrong in itself but becoming so only by the oath, which he had not heard and so had not even consciously transgressed.

Clarke denies the premise of the whole inquiry: Jonathan’s eating the honey was no sin and could not have excited God’s displeasure, since no propitiation was offered for it, no displeasure was manifested, and his own conscience acquits him; the holy oracle told the truth but fixed no blame on him. He assigns two other causes for the silence — that God did not think it proper to send the people out by night, the king’s motive being perfectly vindictive and such a pursuit certain to destroy innocent country people and Israelites living among the Philistines; and that multitudes of the people were at that hour defiled, having eaten the flesh with the blood, and must continue unclean till the evening. He reproduces the substance of the Vulgate and Septuagint addition to the prayer, compares the father’s refusal to break his rash oath with Herod’s beheading of John the Baptist, and frames the rescue as a trial in which the king was judge but the people were the jury, a righteous and impartial jury bringing in a verdict according to the evidence, that no man should die but for a breach of the law of God; God testified no displeasure, and perhaps permitted the whole to correct the king’s propensity to rashness. Wesley makes the silence of the people loyalty, none of those who saw Jonathan eat informing against him because they were satisfied his ignorance excused him and from their great love would not expose him to death for so small an offence; he renders the prayer as a request that God so guide the lot as to discover who is guilty and who innocent, and holds that God so ordered the lot not because he approved the execration or the oath, nor because he would expose Jonathan to death, but that Saul’s folly might be chastised when he saw what danger it had brought on his eldest and excellent son, and that Jonathan’s innocency might be cleared.

A public transgression had been committed and needed special atonement before any answer could come
Not for Jonathan’s honey, which was no sin at all, but because the night pursuit was vindictive and the people were unclean from the blood
It is a case for self-examination: when God denies our prayers we must ask what sin has provoked him

debates.question: Why did none of the people answer the king?

positions.view: Out of loyalty; none who had seen Jonathan eat would inform against him
Out of terror at the king’s word
It was the ominous silence of a horror-stricken people

debates.question: Is the long Greek addition to the lot-casting worth anything?

positions.view: It contains no fact of additional interest
Worth reproducing; its substance is given in full

Alone in making the priest the one man in the army brave enough to withstand the king.

47.pericope_label: A general summary of Saul’s wars on every side, and an account of his house and his captain

schools.summary: Henry reads the closing verses as a general account of the king’s court and camp. Of the family he notes the names of the sons and daughters, the wife, and the cousin who was general of the army, and mentions that a secondary wife appears elsewhere with the children borne to her. Of the camp he observes how the standing army was levied, any strong or valiant man the king saw being taken to himself, exactly as Samuel had warned them the manner of the king would be — and allows that if he must have a standing army it was prudence to fill it with the ablest men he could choose. He supposes the wars to have been defensive, against those who used to invade the borders, the king checking and disappointing them wherever he turned, with the Philistines as the enemy he struggled with most all his days. His conclusion is the hardest line in the section: the king had little reason to be proud of his royal dignity, nor had any of his neighbours cause to envy him, for he had little enjoyment of himself after he took the kingdom and could not vex his enemies without some vexation to himself — such thorns, he says, are crowns quilted with.

Gill explains the taking of the kingdom as a recovery: it had seemed almost taken from him while he was shut up in Gibeah and the Philistines ravaged the country at pleasure, and the victory restored his power and authority, the people submitting readily when they saw him succeed. He gives Kimchi’s sense that he was strengthened in it and the Targum’s that he prospered in it, then reports Abarbanel’s quite different reading, that whereas after his anointing he had followed the herd and attended rustic affairs, he now took upon him the state and majesty of a king and concerned himself no more with his farm and cattle but wholly with regal and military affairs. He reads the gathering of a host as a large army raised because he now had enemies on every side, the earlier levy having been disbanded to three thousand and then to the six hundred who were with him at the last battle. He takes the wife named to have been the mother of all the children listed, and reports Abarbanel’s conjecture that Ishbosheth was borne by another wife, objecting that though Saul had a concubine we nowhere read of a second wife.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that it was by the victory over the Philistines, which drove these obstinate foes back into their own land, that Saul first really acquired the kingship, that is, first secured the regal authority over the Israelites, and insist this is at variance neither with the election by lot nor with the confirmation at Gilgal. They take the phrase rendered he gathered an host for the development and unfolding of power in various respects rather than merely proving himself brave or forming an army, and relate it particularly to the war against Amalek. They note that only three sons are named, those who fell with their father, that the middle name is another name for Abinadab, and that the Chronicles supply a fourth under the form Esh-baal, the reason for the omission being impossible to determine though the name may simply have fallen out in copying; they take the daughters to be named with special reference to the later history, correct the genealogy to read the sons of Abiel rather than the son, and explain the apparent abruptness of the closing notice by making the hardness of the Philistine war the reason for the king’s drawing every strong and brave man to himself. Ellicott names the view that the verse marks the first acquisition of regal authority and prefers another: that it is simply a general view of a reign of perpetual wars, introductory to the list which follows, his argument being the mention of the Ammonite war, which happened considerably earlier and would be out of place unless the whole verse is read as a heading. He maps the enumerated nations as literally surrounding the land, Moab and Ammon east, Edom south, the Philistines west along the Mediterranean, and Zobah a district of Syria to the north-east between the Euphrates and the Orontes. Of the word rendered he vexed them he says the exact sense has puzzled all commentators: the Septuagint evidently read another word and gives he was preserved, the majority of versions and Gesenius yield that wherever he turned he was victorious, and Luther’s rendering, that wherever he turned he inflicted punishment, he calls scholarly and notes that Keil adopts it. He judges the margin’s he wrought mightily more accurate than the received he gathered an host, which follows the Syriac and Vulgate; finds the real difficulty in the list of sons to be the middle name, which occurs nowhere else save in two genealogies as a son of Asher and is supposed to be the Abinadab who fell on Gilboa; takes the daughters to be named for their connection with David’s history; reports the surmise that the queen was of the high priest’s family from the prefix shared by her name and her father’s; cites Ewald’s inference from the plainness of the household that there was this one wife and one concubine only; and credits the reign’s brilliant campaigns in no small measure to the military skill of the general, who after Gilboa was the mainstay of the dead king’s house and over whom David lamented.

Clarke follows the Targum’s sense, that Saul prospered in his government over Israel, and observes that the proofs of his prosperity are immediately subjoined, though of the wars themselves no particulars are given, so that they must have endured a long time and have been in general successful. On the list of sons he reports Calmet’s solution of the absence of Ishbosheth, that he was too young and did not go with his father to the war, only those who went being mentioned, and then demolishes it in a line: why then mention the daughters and the wife, and did they go to the war? Wesley takes the taking of the kingdom as a resumption of the administration, which the Philistines had in a manner turned him out of, and offers Calmet’s explanation of the missing son without misgiving, that only those sons are given who went into these battles and were afterwards slain with their father; he identifies the middle name with Abinadab.

debates.question: What does it mean that Saul took the kingdom?

positions.view: He first really acquired the regal authority by this victory, which is at variance neither with the lot nor with Gilgal
The verse is a general heading to a reign of perpetual wars, as the mention of the earlier Ammonite war shows
He resumed an administration the Philistines had in a manner taken from him
He prospered in his government, with the proofs subjoined

debates.question: Why is Ishbosheth missing from the list of Saul’s sons?

positions.view: Because only the sons who went to the war and fell with their father are named
That answer fails, for the daughters and the wife are named and they did not go to the war
The reason is impossible to determine; the name may simply have fallen out in copying
Abarbanel’s conjecture is that he was borne by another wife — but no second wife is anywhere recorded

debates.question: What does the word rendered he vexed them mean?

positions.view: The sense has puzzled all commentators; Gesenius and most versions give that he was victorious, and Luther’s that he inflicted punishment is scholarly
Luther’s sense is adopted

outliers.claim: Alone in refuting the standard explanation of Ishbosheth’s absence by pointing out that the daughters and the wife are named and did not go to the war.
Alone in reporting Abarbanel’s reading that the king now laid aside his farm and cattle and took on the state and majesty of a king.
Alone in closing the chapter on the cost of the crown, that he could not vex his enemies without some vexation to himself, such thorns being what crowns are quilted with.
